title: The new Eve
hookLine: Irenaeus: the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience

lines: TWO PAGES HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.
cards: Two women, two conversations, far apart in the Bible. In a garden, a woman listens to the serpent and reaches for the fruit.
In a small house in Nazareth, a young woman listens to an angel, and answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
Early Christian writers set those scenes side by side, like two pages held up to the light. One of them, a bishop named Irenaeus, saw a knot in the first and the same knot coming loose in the second.

teach.h: A NEW ADAM, A NEW EVE.
teach.b: You met the new Eve briefly on day three hundred forty; today, the knot. Paul started the pattern. He sets Jesus beside Adam and calls him the last Adam: where the first man brought death, Christ brings life.
Irenaeus took it one step further. If there's a new Adam, isn't there a new Eve beside him? Then the knot.

teach.h: WHAT ONE BOUND, THE OTHER LOOSED.
teach.b: Irenaeus wrote that the knot tied by Eve's disobedience was loosened by Mary's obedience, and that what one virgin bound through unbelief, the other set free through faith.
The Catechism quotes him, and adds his other line: that Mary, by obeying, became a cause of salvation for herself and for the whole human race. Why a knot? In Irenaeus's picture it isn't cut.

teach.h: UNTIED THE WAY IT WAS TIED.
teach.b: It's untied the way it was tied, in reverse. Eve listened to the wrong voice; Mary listens to the right one. Eve doubted the word; Mary trusts it.
Eve reached; Mary receives. The second story walks back through the first, undoing it. Then the name.
In Genesis, Adam names his wife Eve, in the Douay-Rheims, "because she was the mother of all the living."
Christians who call Mary the new Eve hear in her a second mother of the living: mother of the one who is life, and, in Catholic teaching, of everyone who lives in him.

teach.h: BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: None of this makes Mary the savior; the Church is clear that her yes is itself a gift of her son's grace. But it makes her yes enormous.

how: Catholics meet the new Eve in homilies on Mary, and in the Mass readings for the Immaculate Conception, where Genesis 3 is read alongside Luke 1; the Catechism teaches it at paragraph 494.

o: a Christian bride on the day of her wedding
Mary, whose yes undid the knot of Eve's no
Eve, given a fresh start after leaving the garden

games.q: you're Irenaeus. Paul calls Jesus the last Adam. what do you notice?
o: if there's a new Adam, there's a new Eve beside him.
Adam's story should be set aside.
games.why: Irenaeus set Mary beside Eve: what one bound through unbelief, the other set free through faith.

practice: Think of one invitation you've been resisting, a call to return, a task you keep postponing, a kindness you know is being asked of you, and notice the knot of reasons and fear tied around it.
Without forcing anything, picture what one small yes would look like: not the whole thing, one loosened loop. If you pray, borrow Mary's words: be it done to me according to thy word.

wordCard.voice: New Eve. Mary, set beside Eve by early Christian writers: where Eve's no tied the knot, Mary's yes untied it.

orig.note: Hebrew: Eve, the name Genesis ties to her being mother of all the living.

carryVoice: Your line: the knot untied. In this picture, a tangle comes loose the way it was tied, one choice at a time. Another day walked.
